passage:
"Sarika, you're up before me?" said Wasim, rubbing his eyes at the balcony door.
"Watering." She poked a finger into the tin of tulsi. "Still damp. This one can wait." She moved to the marigold tin. "Dry on top. This one gets a mug."
"Why touch the soil every day? Just pour."
"Amma says roots drown if you pour without checking." She tipped the mug slowly. "Two tins, five minutes, then school."
"Fine, fine. Save me a marigold for my shirt pocket."
"They're not for pockets yet." She smiled and picked up her bag.

qa.q: What does Sarika do to check whether a plant needs water?
qa.a: She pokes a finger into the soil.

qa.q: What is Sarika feeling about her plants as she waters them?
qa.a: Caring and content, since she takes her time and smiles as she talks about them.

qa.q: What could Sarika do if she oversleeps one morning, and why?
qa.a: She could ask Wasim to check the soil or water in the evening, so the plants do not go dry.

qa.q: How does Wasim see Sarika's morning routine?
qa.a: Wasim is sleepy and a little amused, teasing her but also asking for a marigold, which shows some interest.

grounding: A girl waters tulsi and marigold each morning before school and checks the soil with a finger first.

subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
passage: I was nine the summer I planted a tulsi and two marigolds in old ghee tins on our balcony. Bhavna-aunty from next door poked holes in the bottoms for me with a nail. The routine was simple, and I kept it the whole term: brush teeth, water plants, then school uniform. But I didn't just pour. First I pushed one finger into the soil, up to the knuckle. If it felt damp, I gave only a little. If it felt dry and crumbly, I gave a whole mug. By the monsoon the tulsi was taller than its tin, and the marigolds were little orange balls. Amma put one on the altar, and I, Parul, stood there feeling ten feet tall.

qa.q: What were the plants grown in?
How did Parul feel when Amma put a marigold on the altar?
qa.a: Parul felt proud and happy, 'ten feet tall'.

qa.q: What would you change in the routine once the monsoon starts?
qa.a: Keep the finger test but expect to water less, since rain keeps the soil damp and too much water can harm the roots.

qa.q: How might Bhavna-aunty see the plants?
qa.a: Bhavna-aunty poked the drainage holes, so Bhavna-aunty would likely be pleased to see the plants thrive.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes a morning watering routine for tulsi and marigold tins, checking the soil with a finger first.

subtype: Approach: following a routine of daily watering [Action]
passage:
Eco-club note, end of July.
Kiran has taken charge of the tulsi and marigold tins on the Class 4 window ledge. Every morning she arrives ten minutes before assembly, puts her bag down and goes straight to the ledge. She does not just tip the bottle. She presses a finger into each tin first. On Monday I heard her say, "This one's still wet from Saturday, only a little." The tin nearest the fan dries faster, and she gives it more. In three weeks the marigolds have four buds. The ones in Class 5, watered "whenever", have yellowed. I have asked Kiran to show the Class 5 monitors her finger test on Friday.
Vijay, eco-club

qa.q: How many buds do the marigolds have?
What does Kiran going straight to the ledge suggest?
qa.a: She feels responsible and protective of the plants, so checking them has become part of her morning.

qa.q: What else could keep the tins healthy over a long holiday?
qa.a: She could ask a classmate or the eco-club to take turns, or move the tins away from the fan so they dry more slowly.

qa.q: What might the Class 5 monitors gain from Friday?
qa.a: Their marigolds yellowed from careless watering, so learning the finger test could save their plants.

grounding: An eco-club note shows a girl watering tulsi and marigold tins every morning before assembly after checking the soil with a finger.
